summary: This document describes a format for logging the secrets used in a TLS connection. Tools can read a file in this format to decrypt captured traffic for diagnosis and debugging. It is intended for systems where TLS only protects test data; because the log file exposes secrets, it should not be used on real traffic.

eli5.summary: If you keep a copy of the key to a locked box, you can open it later and see what happened. This file format is a standard way to save those keys so engineers can debug problems.

subtitle: A standardized format for logging TLS secrets to enable decryption of encrypted traffic.

tldr.problem: When TLS encrypts traffic, diagnostic tools cannot inspect the encrypted messages without the TLS secrets. Developers need a way to record these secrets for debugging without breaking encryption itself.
tldr.mechanism: The SSLKEYLOGFILE format is a plain-text file containing three space-separated fields per line: a label identifying the secret type, the connection's ClientHello random value, and the secret in hexadecimal. Different labels handle TLS 1.3, TLS 1.2, and Encrypted Client Hello (ECH).
tldr.outcome: Tools like Wireshark can use SSLKEYLOGFILE logs to decrypt TLS-protected traffic for analysis. The format is now standardized in RFC 9850. It must only be used for test data due to severe security implications if exposed.

today: RFC 9850 is an IETF Informational RFC published in July 2026. It standardizes a format that has been used informally by TLS implementations since the NSS project. Tools like Wireshark and Firefox use this format to enable developers to decrypt captured TLS traffic for analysis. The format is widely supported and is the standard way to store TLS secrets for debugging purposes.

sections.title: Introduction and Purpose
sections.content:
The SSLKEYLOGFILE format originated in the Network Security Services (NSS) project and has become a de facto standard across TLS implementations. This document formalizes the format that many implementations already use informally.

The format records secrets generated during the TLS key schedule, enabling diagnostic tools to decrypt TLS-protected messages. It supports TLS 1.2, TLS 1.3, DTLS, QUIC, and protocols using the TLS key schedule. The format also covers Encrypted Client Hello (ECH), a TLS extension that encrypts the ClientHello message itself.
sections.eli5: TLS locks up information. SSLKEYLOGFILE writes down the lock combinations so diagnostic tools can look inside later.

sections.title: File Format and Structure
sections.content:
An SSLKEYLOGFILE is a UTF-8 text file with lines terminated by platform-standard line endings. The file contains three space-separated values per secret: a label identifying the secret type, the client_random (the 32-byte Random from ClientHello encoded as 64 hexadecimal characters), and the secret value in hexadecimal.

Empty lines and lines starting with '#' are ignored as comments. Implementations record secrets continuously as they are generated. The format accepts both uppercase and lowercase hexadecimal characters. Each secret occupies a single line, allowing diagnostic tools to parse the file line by line and extract secrets for the connection they are analyzing.
sections.eli5: Each line has three parts separated by spaces: what kind of secret it is, which connection it belongs to (by the random number), and the secret itself written in hex.

sections.title: Secret Labels for TLS 1.3
sections.content:
TLS 1.3 produces multiple secrets through its key schedule. The format defines labels for each: CLIENT_EARLY_TRAFFIC_SECRET (for early data), EARLY_EXPORTER_SECRET (for early exporters), CLIENT_HANDSHAKE_TRAFFIC_SECRET, SERVER_HANDSHAKE_TRAFFIC_SECRET, CLIENT_TRAFFIC_SECRET_0 and SERVER_TRAFFIC_SECRET_0 (protecting application data), and EXPORTER_SECRET (for derived keys). If Encrypted Client Hello was negotiated, these labels must be followed by the Inner ClientHello's Random; otherwise the Outer ClientHello's Random is used.

The labels appear in uppercase in the log file, matching convention while corresponding to lowercase names in the TLS 1.3 specification. Implementations may not log secrets in the order listed here.
sections.eli5: TLS 1.3 creates several different lock keys at different stages. Each has a name like CLIENT_EARLY_TRAFFIC_SECRET so tools know what kind of key they are reading.

sections.title: Security Implications
sections.content:
Access to SSLKEYLOGFILE content completely undermines TLS's confidentiality and integrity protection. The file must be protected with strict access controls. Implementations must ensure logging can only be enabled by authorized users, and files must use appropriate file permissions or equivalent access control.

The format includes secrets that protect record integrity, allowing an attacker to not only read encrypted messages but also inject or modify application data. With TLS 1.2's master secret, an attacker gains the ability to resume connections and impersonate endpoints. Forward secrecy is lost: access to key material allows decryption of previously stored TLS connections. For these reasons, the format is intended only for systems protecting test data, never production systems.
sections.eli5: If someone gets this file, they can read and even modify every encrypted message it covers. It is dangerous and should be kept very safe, and only used for testing.

sections.title: Legacy Support and Extensions
sections.content:
For TLS 1.2 and earlier versions, the format uses the label CLIENT_RANDOM to identify the master secret. The format also extends to Encrypted Client Hello (ECH), a TLS extension that encrypts the Inner ClientHello. Two labels support ECH: ECH_SECRET for the HPKE key encapsulation mechanism shared secret, and ECH_CONFIG for the ECHConfig value used to construct the ECH extension.

The IANA registry created by this RFC reserves space for future labels, using the Specification Required procedure. This allows extensions to cover additional TLS versions and protocols that use the TLS key schedule without modifying this specification.
sections.eli5: Different versions of TLS and extensions like ECH use different kinds of secrets, so the format has different labels for each type, all registered in one place.
